column2: A young sage named Nidagha, a king among sages who had attained knowledge, having been permitted by his father, set out of his own accord on a pilgrimage to holy places.
Having bathed at three and a half crore holy places, he returned home and, bowing to Ribhu, the illustrious one told his own story.

By the merit of bathing at three and a half crore holy places, this reflection arose in my mind:
mahaupanishad:3:4	The world is born and dies, and dies only to be born; all these moving and unmoving activities are unstable; the glorious states of prosperity are the abodes of every calamity.
mahaupanishad:3:5	Like iron rods, unconnected with one another, mere existences dry up through this imagination of the mind.
mahaupanishad:3:6	Aversion to things has come upon me, like a traveler's in a desert; 'How will this sorrow be quenched?' — so my mind burns.
mahaupanishad:3:7	Riches, wheels of heaped-up anxieties, give me no joy; houses with wives and children are like homes of terrible calamities.
mahaupanishad:3:8	Here I stand, in the world, so fragile; O sage, fortune is for delusion, and surely it too gives no peace.
mahaupanishad:3:9	Life is as frail as a drop of water hanging on the tip of a sprout; I would abandon this body like a madman, at the hour of death.
mahaupanishad:3:10	For those who feed on objects, whose minds are worn out by attachment to poison, who lack mature discrimination of the Self, life is a cause of toil.
mahaupanishad:3:11	It is possible to wrap up the wind, to cut the sky, to knot the waves; reliance on life is not possible.
mahaupanishad:3:12	That by which the attainable is attained and one grieves no more, the place of supreme peace — that is called life.
mahaupanishad:3:13	Even trees live, and animals and birds live; but he truly lives whose mind lives by reflection.
mahaupanishad:3:14	Only those creatures in the world have been born who live good lives and are not born here again; the rest are old donkeys.
mahaupanishad:3:15	For the discriminating, scripture is a burden; for the passionate, knowledge is a burden; for the restless, the mind is a burden; for one who does not know the Self, the body is a burden.
mahaupanishad:3:16	Under the sway of egoism come calamities; from egoism, mental anguish; under the sway of egoism comes striving; there is no greater enemy than egoism.
mahaupanishad:3:17	Whatever moving or unmoving thing I have enjoyed through egoism, all that is unreal; the real is emptiness of egoism.
mahaupanishad:3:18	The mind runs here and there, agitated and in vain, going ever farther, like a dog in a village.
mahaupanishad:3:19	By cruel craving, my wife, who follows, I was rendered dull, like one ruled by a dog; O Brahmin, I am free in mind.
mahaupanishad:3:20	Even drinking the ocean, uprooting great Sumeru, or eating fire — O Brahmin, more difficult is the restraint of the mind.
mahaupanishad:3:21	The mind is the cause of things; when it exists the three worlds exist; when it is destroyed the world is destroyed; it must be treated with effort.
mahaupanishad:3:22	Whatever glory of virtue I take refuge in, O best of sages, craving cuts it like a mouse cutting a string.
mahaupanishad:3:23	Satisfied, she makes a nest even on the unscalable; she strives in vain; craving, a restless monkey, does not stay long in one place.
mahaupanishad:3:24	In a moment she goes to the underworld, in a moment to the sky, in a moment wanders in the thickets of the quarters — craving, the bee in the lotus of the heart.
mahaupanishad:3:25	Of all the sorrows of the world, craving alone gives long sorrow, who involves even one in the inner palace in the greatest distress.
mahaupanishad:3:26	The charm against the cholera of craving is the giving up of anxiety, O twice-born; a little brings joy, a little brings weariness.
mahaupanishad:3:27	There is none so pitiable as the body, low and devoid of virtues.
mahaupanishad:3:28	The body is the great house of the householder egoism; let it tumble or become steady — what is that to me, O teacher?
mahaupanishad:3:29	The house of the body, with its row of sense-animals, the courtyard where craving prances, crowded with the mind's servants, I do not want.
mahaupanishad:3:30	The house of the body, fearful at the door of the mouth seized by the monkey of the tongue, with shards of bones for teeth, I do not want.
mahaupanishad:3:31	Of this body made of blood and flesh, outside and inside, whose only nature is destruction — tell me, O sage, what charm does it have?
mahaupanishad:3:32	Whoever has determined permanence in lightning, in autumn clouds, and in cities of gandharvas, may put his trust in the body.
mahaupanishad:3:33	In infancy there is fear of the teacher, of the mother and the father, of people, of elder children; infancy is a house of fear.
mahaupanishad:3:34	The helpless man is overcome by force by the demon of desire, who dwells in the cave of his own mind and makes many delusions.
mahaupanishad:3:35	Servants, sons, wives, kinsmen and friends laugh at the old man trembling with age as at a madman.
mahaupanishad:3:36	Longing, made of misery and fault, grows long in old age, the one companion of all calamities, giving burning in the heart.
mahaupanishad:3:37	Whatever notion of happiness there is in the world, Time, taking it like a stalk of grain, cuts even that.
mahaupanishad:3:38	Time the destroyer of all, bent on making all its own, being self-filling, seizes straw, dust, great Indra, gold, Meru and mustard seed; by it the three worlds are overcome.
mahaupanishad:3:39	What is beautiful in a woman, a doll of flesh, a cage of limbs moving by mechanism, full of sinews, bones and joints?
mahaupanishad:3:40	Separate the skin, flesh, blood, tears and water, and look at the eyes; if you then find it lovely, why are you vainly deluded?
mahaupanishad:3:41	The jewelled necklace, O sage, seen shining on her breast, resembles the rush of the Ganga from the slopes of Meru's peak.
mahaupanishad:3:42	That very breast of a woman, in the cremation grounds and at the ends of the quarters, is in time tasted by dogs like a small ball of rice.
mahaupanishad:3:43	Women with hair like black collyrium, hard to touch, dear to the eye, are flames of the fire of wrong-doing, burning a man like straw.
mahaupanishad:3:44	Even from far away they burn; though juicy they are dry; women are the lovely, terrible fuel of the fires of hell.
mahaupanishad:3:45	Women are the nets, scattered by the hunter named Desire, binding the limbs of the birds who are men with deluded minds.
mahaupanishad:3:46	For the fish of the pond of birth that move in the mud of the mind, woman is the baited hook on the rope of evil impressions.
mahaupanishad:3:47	Enough for me of woman, the casket of all jewels of faults, the ever-chain of sorrow.
mahaupanishad:3:48	He who has a wife has desire for pleasure; for the wifeless, where is the ground of pleasure? Having abandoned woman he has abandoned the world; having abandoned the world he would be happy.
mahaupanishad:3:49	Even the directions are not seen; even the region gives other teaching; mountains crumble and stars decay.
mahaupanishad:3:50	Oceans dry up; even the fixed has an unfixed life; even the perfected perish, and demons and others wear out.
mahaupanishad:3:51	Even the supreme, the steadfast, declines; Hari and the Unborn too; being goes to non-being; the lords of the quarters decay.
mahaupanishad:3:52	Brahma, Vishnu and Rudra, and all classes of beings run only toward destruction, as waters toward the submarine fire.
mahaupanishad:3:53	Calamities come in a moment, prosperity comes in a moment; birth and death in a moment — all that is perishable.
mahaupanishad:3:54	The brave are slain by the unbrave, a hundred by one; poison is the unevenness of sense-objects, what is called poison is not poison.
mahaupanishad:3:55	Objects destroy across births; poison destroys one birth. Thus now in my mind, burnt by the forest-fire of faults,
mahaupanishad:3:56	the hope of pleasures does not stir even in the mirage-lakes. Therefore, O teacher, awaken me quickly with knowledge of truth.
mahaupanishad:3:57	Otherwise I shall take to silence, humble, free of envy, contemplating Vishnu in my mind, like a figure painted in a picture.
mahaupanishad:3:58	Thus the Mahopanishad.
mahaupanishad:4:1	Nidagha, there is nothing else to be known by you, best of the knowing; with the wisdom blessed by the Lord you know. I wipe away the delusion born of the mind's impurity, O sage.
mahaupanishad:4:2	Four gatekeepers at the door of liberation are proclaimed: peace, inquiry, contentment, and fourth, the company of the good.
mahaupanishad:4:3	Or with all effort, giving up all, one should take refuge in one; when one is mastered, all four come under control.
mahaupanishad:4:4	With scriptures, with association with the good, with austerity and self-control, first for liberation from the world, one should increase wisdom itself.
mahaupanishad:4:5	When one's own experience, the scripture and the teacher agree, by practicing which the Self is constantly seen.
mahaupanishad:4:6	If you give up every moment the pursuit of intentions and hopes, you have attained the purifying state of mindlessness.
mahaupanishad:4:7	The mind's non-doership is called samadhi; that alone is aloneness, the supreme bliss that is auspicious.
mahaupanishad:4:8	Abandoning with the mind all contemplation of things as the Self, remain as you are, like one mute, blind and deaf.
mahaupanishad:4:10	All is quiet, unborn, one, without beginning or middle, luminous, mere self-tasting, bearing no mark of the perceived; the view made of the words all is quiet" is only for refutation, and vain: thus this is Om.
You are ever awake in mind, even while performing the world's actions; knowing the oneness of the Self, remain like an unagitated great ocean.
True knowledge is itself the fire for the straw of impressions; it is called samadhi, not mere silent staying.
As the world acts when a jewel stands without desire, so does this host of the world in the supreme principle of mere being.
Therefore, O sage, in the Self there is both doership and non-doership; being without desire it is a non-doer, by mere presence a doer.
Know these two, doership and non-doership, in Brahman, O sage; take refuge in that wherein this wonder is, and be steady.
Therefore contemplate with intelligence "I am ever a non-doer"; that alone remains, called supreme nectar, evenness itself.
Listen, Nidagha: those established in sattva, born on earth with great qualities, are ever risen and joyful, like moons of their own.
They do not sink in calamity, like a golden lotus in the night; they strive for nothing beyond their nature and delight in the path of the good.
They shine by their very form, by conduct of friendliness and other virtues; even, of equal taste, gentle, ever of good conduct.
Like the ocean, of clear minds, they transgress no limit; the great do not abandon their law, like suns.
Who am I, and how is this? — the filth of the world spread out is to be examined with effort by the wise together with the good.
One should not be engaged in evil acts, nor dwell with the ignoble; the destroyer of all is to be seen; death is not to be scorned.
Giving up the body as bones and flesh and the unlovely blood and the rest, one should see pure consciousness, the thread of the garland of pearls of the elements.
The inclination toward what is to be accepted and the complete dismissal of what is to be given up — know that to be the mind's form, external, and not otherwise.
By the path taught by teacher and scripture and by one's own experience, knowing "I am Brahman" in the mass of consciousness, the sage becomes free of sorrow.

Where one must endure like the falling of a hundred sharp swords and the striking of lotuses, burning by fire like sprinkling with snow, rolling on coals like smearing with sandalwood, the shower of endless arrows like the sprinkling of a fountain in a summer-house, the cutting off of one's own head like pleasant sleep, dumbness like a seal on the mouth, deafness like great gain — one should not treat this with contempt; thus from firm dispassion arises knowledge. By pure self-experience born of the teacher's words and practice, the Self is constantly seen.
Even for one whose confusion of direction is gone, the direction appears as before; so contemplate that the world, destroyed by knowledge, does not exist.
Neither riches nor friends nor kinsmen help; neither the lack of bodily suffering nor reliance on pilgrimage places; the state is attained only by that which is made of the mind alone.
All sorrows, unbearable craving, and anguish vanish in tranquil minds like darkness in the suns.
As toward a mother, all beings here trust the one who has peace, both the rough and the soft.
A man attains happiness not by drinking elixirs nor by Lakshmi's embrace as he does by inner peace.
He who, having heard, touched, eaten, seen, known good or bad, neither rejoices nor sinks, is tranquil.
He whose mind, clear like the moon's disc, is unperturbed in death, festivals and battles is tranquil.
Among ascetics, scholars, sacrificers, kings, the strong and the virtuous, only the peaceful shines.
Those tranquil ones who are satisfied with drinking the nectar of contentment, delighting in the Self, great souls, have attained the great state.
He who has abandoned the unattained and is equal in what is attained, who knows neither the pain of the unseen nor lack of pain — he is contented.
He who does not rejoice at what is not obtained, and enjoys what is obtained as he wishes, of gentle conduct — he is contented.
The wise one delights in what is attained, like a faithful wife in the inner courtyard; that state of liberation-while-living arises, giving the bliss of one's own nature.
According to the moment, the scripture, the place, the comfort, as company of the good is possible — this order of the path of liberation, the wise should consider until rest is found in the Self.
For one endowed with rest in the Fourth, turned back from the ocean of becoming, living or not living, householder or ascetic;
there is no purpose in what is done or not done, nor in confusion of scripture and tradition; like an ocean without a churning-rod, he stays as he is.
When the pure knowledge of the Self as all arises, your own self shines, outside of space and time, of the form of consciousness, as the body.
Thus the Self, as it manifests wherever, stays there swiftly and shines in that very form.
